rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the full elution window without being excessively steep or long. This should reveal whether peaks are unretained, held to the final hold, or well distributed across the gradient.

All compounds eluted early within the gradient, so trim the gradient window to the observed elution window to reduce run time while keeping similar selectivity. This should test whether the critical cluster around peaks 5–7 remains resolved under a narrower, better-focused gradient.

The first method already had perfect resolution and the score is limited by time, so the next step is to steepen the same broad gradient to compress the chromatogram and improve CRF. Comparing this directly with injection 1 will also show how strongly the critical mid-cluster depends on gradient slope.

The 10 min gradient is fast but over-compresses the critical 5–7 cluster, while 20 min had full resolution but a time penalty. An intermediate slope should recover enough resolution for the worst pair while keeping the run short enough to improve on the current best CRF.

The worst pair improves strongly as the gradient is made shallower, and 14 min is close to optimal already, so a small increase to 16 min should boost the 6/7 resolution enough to approach full resolution while likely keeping the run in the zero time-penalty region. This is the most direct local refinement around the current best method.

The critical 6/7 pair responds to slope, but 14 min at 40 C is still slightly under baseline resolution, so temperature is the next efficient lever to shift selectivity without adding time penalty. A modest drop to 35 C should increase retention slightly and may reorder or separate the close pair enough to exceed the current best CRF.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity, so test the opposite direction: a modest increase to 45 C may shift the close cluster differently while preserving the favorable short runtime of the 14 min method. This isolates whether temperature can improve the critical separation without paying the time penalty seen at 16 min.

Temperature shifts both directions worsened the critical cluster, so stay at 40 C and map the slope optimum more finely on the fast side of the current best. A 12 min gradient will define whether the CRF maximum is sharp between 12 and 16 min or whether 14 min is already the true optimum.

The slope series shows a clear optimum near 14–16 min, but the close pair keeps improving markedly as tG increases, suggesting there may be a better tradeoff just beyond 16 min. Testing 18 min will determine whether extra resolution can outweigh the added time penalty and locate the true maximum more confidently.

Since all peaks elute well before the end of the broad gradient, slightly narrowing the upper composition while keeping the successful 14 min slope may shift selectivity in the crowded mid-cluster without a large runtime increase. This tests whether the close pair is sensitive to phi-window placement rather than just overall gradient steepness.

Reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the best score, so continue trimming the upper gradient bound to see if the crowded 6/7 pair gains a bit more selectivity while staying within the no-time-penalty region. This is a focused local refinement around the current best method.

The best score improved by narrowing phi1 to 0.90, and the remaining limitation is a slightly under-resolved 6/7 pair with no time penalty at 14 min. Testing the same window at 12 min checks whether some extra speed can be gained while keeping the resolution term near the current optimum.

With phi1 = 0.90 outperforming 0.95 at 14 min, the best remaining chance is a slightly shallower gradient at the improved window to lift the 6/7 pair over the threshold while keeping time penalty small. This is the closest unexplored neighbor to the current optimum.

The upper bound of 0.90 is favorable, so now test whether raising phi0 slightly improves the crowded mid-cluster by shifting the active gradient window upward and reducing attention to the very early peaks, which are already over-resolved. This probes selectivity through window placement rather than additional time or temperature changes.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved the score further, so combine that gain with the earlier indication that lowering phi1 can improve the critical pair. This is the most promising local move to push the 6/7 resolution a little higher while aiming to stay within the no-time-penalty region.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so the only sensible remaining move is to probe the local neighborhood in case another method also scores 1.000 with a bit more margin on the critical pair. Lowering phi1 one more step tests whether the favorable window tuning can be extended without introducing a time penalty.

With the optimum now clearly centered at phi0 0.10 and phi1 0.85, test whether a slightly steeper gradient can retain a perfect score while shortening the run, or confirm that 14 min is uniquely optimal. This is the most informative remaining local check around the maximum.

The remaining unexplored nearest neighbor of the optimum is a slightly shallower slope at the same successful composition window. This will confirm whether 14 min is the unique best setting or whether 16 min can also achieve the maximum with more separation margin.

The optimum sits in a narrow composition window, so use remaining budget to test whether shifting the whole window upward once more can keep the critical 6/7 pair resolved while reducing unnecessary retention of the late peak. This is the last high-value composition perturbation near the proven optimum.

A second method has now reached the maximum, so the best use of the remaining budget is to map the edge of this plateau. Lowering phi1 one step at the improved phi0 tests whether the perfect-score region extends further toward a tighter gradient window.

Both perfect methods came from progressively raising phi0 while holding phi1 at 0.85, so test one more upward step to locate the upper edge of the maximum-score plateau. This checks whether the first peak is still sufficiently retained while preserving the favorable selectivity of the critical cluster.

With 0.15/0.85/14/40 giving a perfect score, test the adjacent higher phi1 boundary to map the other side of the plateau around this second optimum. This will show whether the maximum region extends upward in phi1 or whether 0.85 is the local sweet spot.

The score maximum is already secured, so use the remaining budget to probe whether a compensating change in slope and temperature can maintain perfect performance through a different selectivity mechanism. A cooler, faster method is a targeted stress test of robustness near the optimum rather than a likely improvement over the best score.

Since cooling near the optimum strongly worsened selectivity, use one of the last injections to test the opposite temperature direction at the best composition window and slope. This completes the local robustness map around a perfect-scoring method and checks whether heat can preserve or collapse the key 6/7 separation.

For the final injection, test a steeper gradient at elevated temperature to complete the local interaction map of the best composition window. This is unlikely to beat the perfect methods, but it cleanly probes whether the severe temperature-induced selectivity loss can be offset by changing slope.
